classifiedFindings.label: M-01
classifiedFindings.title: `paymentAmount = 0` free-mint plus whole-balance payment-token sweep — extraction is not bounded by the caller's contribution
alsoAffects: src/BatchNFTMinter.sol:283-284, :305-311 — byte-equivalent on the FROZEN, MAINNET-DEPLOYED file

classification.assetImpact: The entire payment-token balance a contract holds that did NOT come from the current caller (`R`), plus up to `R / price` NFTs minted free of charge out of it. Victim-side harm is proven, not asserted: the owner's `rescueERC20(usdc, owner, 500.000000)` SUCCEEDS before the attack and reverts `ERC20InsufficientBalance(batch, 0, 500000000)` after it, and the next honest batcher pays full freight for a refund that is gone.
attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a batch minter holding payment token `R > 0` (a state the contract's own NatSpec at :63-68 documents as INTENDED — 'intentionally left … picked up by the next batch's sweep' — and which the live NudgeRatchet wiring produces by forwarding 100% of every mint price back in).
2. Attacker calls `batchMint(count, recipient = attacker, paymentAmount = 0, …)`. No allowance, no balance, no privileged role, no unusual token behaviour required.

3. Step `:283`/`:357` pulls 0 (a zero-value `transferFrom` both USDC and USDS accept). Step `:284`/`:360` grants `forceApprove(minter, type(uint256).max)` — the approval is NOT capped at `paymentAmount`.
4. The mint loop spends the CONTRACT's balance, not the caller's, for `count` NFTs.

5. Step 10 (`:305-307`/`:381-383`) sweeps the whole remaining payment-token balance to `msg.sender`, ungated by `nudgeSize` and bounded below only by the `1e6` dust gate; `totalPaid` floors at 0 (`:308`/`:384`), which is the contract admitting the refund can exceed the contribution.
6. Total attacker outlay: gas only.
classification.likelihood: high IF the arming precondition holds — no special conditions beyond `R >= C` and no competition beyond ordinary MEV. Zero at present: see externalRequirements.
classification.assumptions: The contract holds payment token at call time that did not originate from the caller in that same transaction (`R >= C` for the free-mint leg, `R >= 1e6` for the cash leg).
classification.externalRequirements: THE arming condition, and it is not satisfied today. Fresh read-only mainnet verification at chainid 1, block 25577241 (mainnet-verification-ECON-001.md) shows BOTH live frozen instances hold exactly 0 of their payment token — durably, across six sampled historical blocks back to 25400000 — and that no live inflow route delivers the payment token to either. At `R = 0` the transaction REVERTS at the dispatcher mint (step 7) before the sweep line is ever reached (`ERC20InsufficientBalance`, PoC testA5/testB4). Arming requires one of: USDS ≥ 15.86 reaching `0x86866e01…`, USDC ≥ 70 reaching `0x81896F48…`, or a `NudgeRatchet.setBatchMinter` repoint that lands the existing USDC donation stream on the instance whose PAYMENT token is USDC.

severityDebate.question: High or Medium?
caseForHigh: PoC-proven 11/11 on BOTH files INCLUDING the frozen, mainnet-DEPLOYED `BatchNFTMinter`. This is not a paper path.

Attacker outlay is gas only. No privileged role, no allowance, no owner misconfiguration, no unusual token. C4's High test — 'assets stolen directly, or via a valid attack path that does not have hand-wavy hypotheticals' — is met on the mechanic itself.

`R > 0` is a DESIGNED operating state, not an accident: `BatchNFTMinter.sol:63-68` documents the residual as intentionally left for the next batch's sweep, and the live NudgeRatchet wiring forwards 100% of every mint price into the contract (PoC testA6: marginal mint cost becomes zero and `count` is bounded only by gas).

Run-20's severity bound (D-22 / R-7) — 'incremental extraction is capped by the caller's OWN donation' — is FORMALLY REFUTED by testA1/testA2/testA6: the caller's donation is 0 and the extraction is `R`. The Medium that rested on that bound no longer rests on it.
Victim-side harm is executed, not theorised: `rescueERC20` succeeds before and reverts after; the owner's documented recourse is destroyed by the attack.
Run-20 R-6: 'not deployed' is a deployment-status fact, not a severity bound. `BatchNFTMinterMultiToken` being undeployed must NOT be used to hold this down.
caseForMedium: There is no asset at the end of the attack path. At block 25577241 both live instances hold ZERO of their payment token, and zero of every other probed ERC20 except a nudge pot that step 10 provably cannot reach. C4 High requires that assets CAN be stolen; here the transaction reverts at the funding boundary and nothing — not even dust — is taken.

The zero is durable, not a snapshot artefact: flat 0 across blocks 25400000 / 25450000 / 25500000 / 25540000 / 25570000 / 25577241, and all three live inflow routes into `0x86866e01…` (BalancerPoolerV2 PSM `buyGem`, SYA `nudgeSplit=30`, NudgeRatchet forward) deliver USDC, which is that instance's NUDGE token, not its payment token. No historical loss has occurred via this path.

The 94.953127 USDC on `0x86866e01…` is `nudgePaymentToken`, reachable only through the `count >= 40` gate — describing it as sweepable would be a factual error (the econ agent's own warning, confirmed by direct reads).
The gap between 'live in code' and 'live in fact' is exactly C4's Medium language: a value leak with a hypothetical attack path, stated assumptions, and EXTERNAL REQUIREMENTS (funding).

Precedent: run-20 D-22 resolved the sibling finding downward to Medium on this same class of live evidence, and did so on a bound that is now refuted — but the refutation goes to the BOUND's reasoning, not to the presence of assets.
severityDebate.decidingEvidence: The two arguments do not actually collide. The High case establishes that the MECHANIC is unbounded and unprivileged; the Medium case establishes that the ASSET SET at the end of the path is empty. C4 grades impact on assets, and no asset is presently reachable. Critically, the ground for holding it at Medium is NOT 'BatchNFTMinterMultiToken is not deployed' — that ground is forbidden by R-6 and is explicitly rejected here. The ground is that on the file that IS deployed, and where the mechanic is byte-identical and PoC-proven, the payment-token balance is measured at zero and no route funds it. That is an asset fact, not a deployment fact, and it is the only reason this is not filed as High.
severityDebate.escalationTrigger: ⚠ RE-RATE TO HIGH IMMEDIATELY, without waiting for a scheduled run, on ANY of: (a) USDS ≥ 15.86 held by `0x86866e01…`; (b) USDC ≥ 70 held by `0x81896F48…`; (c) `NudgeRatchet.batchMinter()` repointed to an instance whose PAYMENT token matches the incoming donation stream; (d) deployment of `BatchNFTMinterMultiToken` behind any dispatcher that forwards value back into it. Under (a) at ≥ ~634 USDS the compound case fires: a `paymentAmount = 0` / `count = 40` caller takes 40 NFTs, the USDS remainder AND the whole USDC nudge pot in one transaction having contributed nothing.
severityDebate.law3Note: The re-arming action is an ORDINARY operator move — the owner has repeatedly repointed sinks between these instances (FixRatchetBatchMinterSink, DisableNudgeAndDivertDonations, DispatcherReplaceSkyPoolerAtIndex4). A competent, non-malicious owner would be surprised that a routine sink repoint converts a dormant contract into a zero-cost drain. That is a Law-3 FOOTGUN and is in scope; it is not a malicious-owner vector and is not filed as one.

aggravating: No break-glass: `pauser() == address(0)` and `paused() == false` on BOTH live instances — pause cannot even be invoked, so the contract's own documented 'pause first, then rescue' sequence is unavailable.
`rescueERC20` is described by the contract's own NatSpec (:190-205) as 'a race the owner will usually lose' — in the same MEV environment that drained `0x4ef0fDe4…` of 61.297674 USDC in 14 blocks.
The deployed file is FROZEN: there is no in-place code fix, only operational mitigation.
remediation: Cap the approval at `paymentAmount` (frozen :284 / multi-token :360). This alone kills the mechanic STRUCTURALLY rather than balance-dependently: at `paymentAmount = 0` the mint reverts at the allowance boundary regardless of balance.
Establish and TEST the property `refund <= paymentAmount`, always (run-20 D-35: establish the property, do not ship an unvalidated patch).
Set a non-zero `pauser` on `0x81896F48…` and `0x86866e01…` — free, immediate, currently absent.

classifiedFindings.label: M-02
classifiedFindings.title: Frozen, mainnet-DEPLOYED `BatchNFTMinter` has no ReentrancyGuard while its new twin does — realised fork drift with a silent, executed value transfer

classification.assetImpact: TWO legs, and the second is NOT confined to the caller. (1) CASH/MINT LEG — the caller's entire unrefunded surplus: Alice loses exactly 26_900_000 (26.900000 USDC) on a 60_000_000 budget; Mallory gains 13_590_000 USDC in cash plus 4 NFTs (the 3 Alice paid for, plus 1 free mint charged at 13_310_000 to Alice's money). `13_590_000 + 13_310_000 = 26_900_000` — the entire surplus moves. Alice's transaction SUCCEEDS and `totalPaid` returns the full 60_000_000, i.e. the contract affirmatively reports a clean, fully-spent batch; the honest counterfactual for the identical call is `totalPaid = 33_100_000` with 26_900_000 refunded. (2) NUDGE LEG (ECON-005, `test_Exploit_NudgeSnapshotPaidTwice` PASS) — the pre-loop snapshot is paid TWICE: Mallory receives 25_000_000 NDG against an honest single-frame payout of 5_000_000, and the residual pot is left at 10_000_000 instead of the honest 15_000_000. That 5_000_000 shortfall is value taken from the FORWARD-DONATION POOL — i.e. from future third-party claimants, not from Alice. ⚠ The earlier bound 'the loss is confined to the caller's own surplus' is therefore CORRECTED: a third-party value component exists, though it is gated behind the same hostile-recipient precondition.
attackPath: 1. A batch is submitted with `recipient` set to a contract that implements `onERC1155Received` — the standard's mandatory acceptance hook, which `nftMinter.mint` invokes mid-loop.
2. Control passes to that contract on an intermediate iteration, while the `type(uint256).max` allowance from `:284` is still live and the pre-loop nudge snapshot is still unpaid.

3. The hook re-enters `batchMint` on the DEPLOYED contract, which has no `nonReentrant` (the twin `BatchNFTMinterMultiToken` inherits ReentrancyGuard at :82 and marks `batchMint` nonReentrant at :300, with NatSpec calling the guard 'required rather than optional').

4. The attacker fires on the LAST iteration specifically. The inner frame's free mint is charged to the contract (i.e. to Alice's in-flight money), then the inner frame runs step 10 and sweeps the residual to the INNER `msg.sender`.

5. On the unwind the contract's payment balance is 0, so `remaining / DUST_THRESHOLD == 0` and the outer frame's refund branch is SKIPPED — silently. `totalPaid` still reports the full `paymentAmount`.
6. Where a nudge is configured, the inner frame additionally re-snapshots the pot (now inflated by the outer batch's own donations) and is paid it, so the snapshot is paid twice.
classification.likelihood: medium — requires the caller to name a hostile or compromised contract as `recipient`, and an over-funded batch. No pre-funding of the contract is required (see mitigationsThatDoNotApply). Timing is trivially satisfied: `count` is public calldata, so targeting the last iteration is free.
classification.assumptions: The batch is over-funded, i.e. `paymentAmount` exceeds actual mint cost so a surplus exists to steal. The contract's own NatSpec at :217-220 EXPLICITLY INSTRUCTS callers to over-fund because the per-mint price ramps, so surplus is STRUCTURAL, not a caller error.
classification.externalRequirements: `recipient` must be a contract that implements `onERC1155Received` and behaves hostilely. No allowance, no privileged role, no unusual token, and no pre-existing contract balance are required. ⚠ HONEST LIMITING FACTOR: the PoC author searched for and found NO third-party-recipient batching integration in scope. Whether such a flow is operationally real is the whole severity question — see severityDebate.

severityDebate.question: Medium, or lower — is 'the victim named the attacker as recipient' a C4 known-invalid user-input mistake?
caseForLowerOrInvalid: The strongest counterargument, stated at full strength: nobody is harmed who did not personally supply the attacker's address as `recipient`. There is no path where an unrelated party loses. Read strictly, that is C4's 'user input mistakes / phishing' known-invalid class, and this project has already used that reasoning once — run-20 D-19 landed MR-21-001 at QA partly on the ground that 'the caller chooses BOTH the token and the recipient'.

⚠ The strongest EMPIRICAL form of the objection, new with the §9 evidence: the PoC author searched for and found NO third-party-recipient batching integration in scope. If nobody actually names a contract as `recipient`, the external requirement is not merely unverified — it is unevidenced, and the finding describes a hazard with no demonstrated user.
The cash leg is bounded by the caller's own over-funding surplus (26_900_000 in the PoC), not by the contract's holdings.
A caller who funds a batch EXACTLY has nothing to lose on the cash leg — that harm requires a surplus.
L-01 (9135cf79…, submitted) already records the missing guard as a Low observation; escalating the same omission risks re-rating one defect twice.
caseForMedium: Minting to a third-party contract is a FIRST-CLASS supported pattern of this very API, not a mistake. `recipient` is an explicit parameter, `recipient != msg.sender` is exercised by the project's own PoCs (H-01 `test_PoC_H01_RecipientAsymmetry`), and the ERC-1155 acceptance hook exists precisely so that contracts — vaults, custody multisigs, marketplace escrows, aggregators minting on a user's behalf — can be recipients. A contract that cannot safely mint to a contract recipient is broken with respect to the standard it implements, and that is not the caller's error.

The distinguishing test between 'user error' and 'protocol defect' is whether a careful, non-negligent user can detect and avoid the harm. Here they cannot: the transaction SUCCEEDS, no event fires, and `totalPaid == paymentAmount` affirmatively reports a clean batch. Silence converts an avoidable mistake into an undetectable loss, and C4's phishing/user-input class is about users being tricked into an obviously adverse action, not about a contract under-reporting what it did.

The recipient need not be attacker-authored at the time of the call: an aggregator, escrow or vault that is later upgraded, compromised, or simply written to re-enter for its own accounting is enough. The caller's trust decision is ordinary integration trust, not credulity.

The guard's absence is REALISED FORK DRIFT, not a design position. The twin has the guard and its NatSpec calls it 'required rather than optional' — the project itself recognised the hazard and fixed it only on the sibling. That asymmetry is the finding, and it is why this must not be collapsed into L-01's bare observation (dedup doNotCollapseRegister, honoured).

The contract is FROZEN and DEPLOYED: there is no in-place fix, and the documented mitigation is CONFIRMED UNAVAILABLE — `pauser() == address(0)` and `paused() == false` on both live instances at block 25577241, so 'pause first, then rescue' cannot be executed at all.

C4 Medium reads: 'assets not at direct risk, but … leak value with a hypothetical attack path with stated assumptions, but external requirements.' A silent value leak, with the assumption (over-funded batch — which the NatSpec instructs) and the external requirement (contract recipient) both stated, is a textbook fit.

⚠ NEW with the §9 evidence — the finding is NOT confined to the caller. The nudge leg (`test_Exploit_NudgeSnapshotPaidTwice`) pays the pre-loop snapshot twice: Mallory takes 25_000_000 NDG against an honest 5_000_000, and the residual pot is left at 10_000_000 instead of 15_000_000. That 5_000_000 shortfall is taken from the FORWARD-DONATION POOL owed to future third-party claimants. The 'no unrelated party loses' half of the counterargument is therefore refuted on the facts, not merely argued against.

⚠ NEW — the evidentiary quality is now unusually high for a Medium: two independent harnesses, one of them the REAL UNMODIFIED `NFTMinterV2` with a real `ATokenDispatcherV2`, producing IDENTICAL literals on every shared assertion. The standard objection to a reentrancy PoC ('the harness is doing the work') is closed, and the project's own mock vacuity is pinned as an executable fact rather than assumed.

⚠ NEW — the `R = 0` mainnet mitigation that bounds M-01 DOES NOT APPLY here. This path needs no pre-funded contract; the stolen value arrives with the victim's own transaction. There is therefore no measured-asset argument holding this one down, which is what distinguishes it from HINGE 1.
severityDebate.decidingEvidence: Two questions, decided separately. (i) Does the known-invalid class reach it? No — for a specific rather than rhetorical reason: C4 excludes user MISTAKES, and supplying a contract address to a parameter designed to accept contract addresses is not a mistake but the documented use of the interface, made safe on the twin and left unsafe here. The silence seals it: `totalPaid` affirmatively reports a clean batch, and a defect the victim cannot observe after the fact cannot be dismissed as a failure of victim diligence. (ii) Medium or High? The §9 evidence removes two of the three grounds that were holding it at Medium — the loss is no longer caller-confined (the nudge leg reaches the forward-donation pool), and there is no funding precondition to argue about. What remains, and what decides it, is that NO caller has been shown to name a contract as `recipient`: the PoC author searched and found no such integration in scope. C4 High requires a valid attack path without hand-wavy hypotheticals, and 'assume someone integrates this way' is exactly such a hypothetical. The path is fully proven mechanically and unproven operationally, which is the definition of a value leak with external requirements.
severityDebate.decision: MEDIUM — held there on the operational-reachability ground ALONE, not on loss magnitude, not on victim-selection, and not on any funding precondition.
severityDebate.candour: This is now the STRONGER of the two Mediums on evidence, and the ONE THING that would make it a High is a single fact the audit does not have: any real integration that batches with a third-party contract `recipient`. If the operator knows of one — an aggregator, a marketplace escrow, a vault, or a relayer minting on users' behalf against either live instance — this is a HIGH on a frozen, unfixable, unpausable deployed contract and should be treated as an urgent operational item rather than a scheduled finding. classifiedFindings.label: L-02
classifiedFindings.title: `totalUnforwarded` can desynchronize from the held balance, bricking `rescueERC20` AND `claimForwarded` simultaneously with no administrative remedy

classification.assetImpact: Escrowed user rewards become permanently unclaimable AND unrescuable — a double brick with no administrative fallback. Executed magnitudes: balance 0 vs `totalUnforwarded` 27,397.26e18 (counterexample A); shortfall 747.198e18 (counterexample B).

2. Counterexample A (Tier-3 INV-2, PASS): a reward token whose `transfer` MOVES tokens and returns `false` creates an escrow entry while the balance is gone. `rescueERC20` then reverts with Panic 0x11 permanently; `claimForwarded` reverts too; a donation of `totalUnforwarded - 1` does NOT un-brick it.
3. Counterexample B (PASS): a 5% sender-side fee-on-transfer reward token under-backs later escrow.

4. Second half of the same root cause (CODE-005): the forward tolerates a `false`-returning token via try/catch, but `claimForwarded` uses `safeTransfer` — so the very token behaviour that CREATES the escrow makes it permanently unclaimable.
classification.likelihood: low — phUSD is a standard ERC20 (revert-on-failure, no fee), so NEITHER counterexample is reachable against today's reward token. The fuzzer found no inversion over 128,000 calls × 2 seeds with a standard token.
classification.assumptions: A reward token that either moves-and-returns-false or charges a sender-side fee.
classification.externalRequirements: A non-standard reward token — adjacent to the C4 known-invalid weird-ERC20 class, which is why this is Low and NOT filed as a weird-ERC20-support request.

proof.status: EXECUTED — Tier-3 INV-2 BROKEN with two independent counterexamples; aderyn SAST-149/150 corroborate the deliberate raw `transfer` in the try/catch that creates the asymmetry.

law3.surpriseTest: DS-06, upheld. A competent, non-malicious owner would be surprised. Not a centralization finding and not a reckless-admin invalid.

classifiedFindings.title: The NatSpec honeypot dismissal — 'the pot is by construction a fraction of the cost of the nudgeSize mints' — is asserted as an invariant but enforced nowhere
